title: SQL Fundamentals
tagline: Constraints, normalization, views and row-level security — data integrity as architecture

placementQuiz.q: Which constraint type can forbid overlapping bookings?
placementQuiz.explain: An exclusion constraint can compare ranges for overlap; CHECK can't see other rows.

placementQuiz.q: An FK drops the dependent rows when the parent goes away. Which clause encodes that?
placementQuiz.explain: ON DELETE CASCADE propagates deletion to referencing rows.

placementQuiz.q: Normalizing a table with repeating (supplier, price) per product — the supplier+price block typically becomes…
options: A child table keyed to the product
placementQuiz.explain: Repeating groups belong in a related child table (1NF→2NF breakdown).

options: run checks against the calling user's privileges
placementQuiz.explain: Without it, views run with the view owner's rights; security_invoker re-checks the caller.

placementQuiz.q: RLS is enabled but not FORCEd; what reverts for table owners and superusers?
options: Superusers and table owners bypass unless FORCE ROW LEVEL SECURITY
placementQuiz.explain: FORCE makes the policy apply even to the table owner.

blocks.md: **A schema is a contract the database enforces for you. Constraints, normalization, and row-level security turn intentions into guarantees.**

Beyond `PRIMARY KEY`, the database can enforce domain rules (`CHECK`), row uniqueness (`UNIQUE`), referential integrity (`FOREIGN KEY`), and even cross-row relationships (`EXCLUDE` on GiST). Each one makes a guarantee that application code inherits — a bad row simply cannot be written.

blocks.label: check, unique, fk (PostgreSQL)
blocks.pg:
-- REFERENCES creates a foreign key; ON DELETE CASCADE removes
-- the referring rows together with the parent

blocks.label: fk actions and deferrable
blocks.pg: -- DEFERRABLE INITIALLY DEFERRED is checked at COMMIT (PostgreSQL)
blocks.mysql:
-- MySQL 8.0 has no DEFERRABLE constraints; FK checks run per
-- statement immediately, so insert order matters

blocks.label: exclusion constraints (EXCLUDE USING gist)
blocks.code:
CREATE EXTENSION IF NOT EXISTS btree_gist;  -- needed for = on room_id

CREATE TABLE reservations (
  room_id int NOT NULL,
  slot_tsrange tsrange NOT NULL,
  EXCLUDE USING gist (
    room_id WITH =,
    slot_tsrange WITH &&
  )
);

-- '&&' means overlaps: inserting a conflicting row raises an error.
-- Caveat: EXCLUDE is PostgreSQL-only, and using = on an ordinary
-- scalar column requires the btree_gist extension.
blocks.pg: -- tsrange is a built-in range type; && is the range-overlap operator
blocks.mysql:
-- MySQL 8.0 has no EXCLUDE / USING gist. Emulate exclusion rules
-- with application-side locking or a trigger over the table

items.q: A DEFERRABLE INITIALLY DEFERRED foreign key is enforced:
options: Only when the parent table is locked
At COMMIT, not at statement end
items.explain: Deferrable constraints delay the check to the end of the transaction, so insertion order inside a transaction no longer matters.

items.q: Which constraint can compare data across different rows?
items.explain: CHECK evaluates one row's expression; only an exclusion constraint can reject a row that overlaps an existing row.

blocks.md: Normalization removes redundancy by splitting tables until each fact lives in exactly one place. **1NF**: atomic values, no repeating groups. **2NF**: no partial dependencies — a column must describe the whole key, not just part of it. **3NF**: no transitive dependencies — a non-key column's only dependency is the key. Denormalization is the deliberate inverse: folding tables back together on read-hot reporting paths (star schemas with fact + dimension tables), trading write-side elegance for fewer joins at query time.

blocks.label: violating 1NF — repeating product block
blocks.code:
-- product/supplier facts repeat on every order line
CREATE TABLE orders_1nf (
  order_id      int,
  product_id    int,
  product_name  text,
  price         numeric,
  supplier_name text
);

-- product_name and supplier_name depend on product_id, not on the
-- whole key (order_id, product_id) — a partial dependency, the 2NF
-- violation. The repeating block belongs in a child table.

blocks.label: the normalized split
blocks.pg:
-- supplier name now lives only in suppliers (3NF: no transitive
-- product → supplier → supplier_name dependency)
blocks.mysql: -- Same DDL is valid in MySQL 8.0

blocks.label: denormalized reporting row (deliberate choice)
blocks.code:
-- READ path: re-join dimensions for a report
SELECT s.order_id, p.name, sup.name, p.price, s.qty
FROM   order_lines s
JOIN   products    p   ON p.id  = s.product_id
JOIN   suppliers   sup ON sup.id = p.supplier_id;

-- On a hot analytics path you may pre-join into a fact table
-- (denormalization): storage cost for fewer joins per query.
-- It is a reporting trade-off, not a substitute for constraints.
blocks.pg: -- star-schema fact tables + dimension tables is the classic shape
blocks.mysql: -- MySQL 8.0: materialized fact tables are app-maintained

items.q: orders_1nf stores (order_id, product_id, product_name, price, supplier_name). Repeating product facts per order violate:
options: 2NF — a partial dependency on part of the composite key
3NF — a transitive dependency through the key
No normal form — it is already normalized
items.explain: product_name and supplier_name depend on product_id, not the whole (order_id, product_id) key — a partial dependency, removed at 2NF.

items.q: Why denormalize in a star schema?
options: Fewer joins on read-heavy analytics, better reporting latency
It reduces storage to a minimum
It runs identically on every engine
items.explain: Pre-joined fact tables trade write-side elegance and storage for faster reads on hot reporting paths.

blocks.text: Views are Stored Queries; RLS is Per-Row Filtering

blocks.label: a simple view
blocks.pg:
-- A view is a named query; simple single-table views are
-- flattened into the outer query by the planner
blocks.mysql: -- MySQL views behave the same; simple views are inlined

blocks.label: security_invoker (PostgreSQL 15+)
blocks.code:
-- By default a view runs with its OWNER's privileges, which can
-- leak rows the caller could not read directly.
-- security_invoker re-checks the calling user at every access:
CREATE VIEW v_customers
WITH (security_invoker = true) AS
SELECT * FROM customers;
blocks.pg:
-- Without security_invoker, a user granted SELECT on the view may
-- see rows they cannot read from the base table directly
blocks.mysql:
-- MySQL views execute with the DEFINER's privileges; there is no
-- SECURITY INVOKER option. Separate per-tenant views are the usual
-- workaround

blocks.label: row-level security policy
blocks.pg:
-- current_setting('app.tenant_id')::int reads a session GUC set
-- per request, e.g. SET app.tenant_id = 7;
blocks.mysql:
-- MySQL 8.0 has no row-level security; emulate with per-tenant
-- views or app-level filters

blocks.md: **RLS filters rows — it does not grant table access.** If the user cannot reach the table at all, policies never run. The two checks layer: privileges (can you touch the table?) then policies (which rows may you see?).

items.q: A query against a simple single-table view usually shows the base table directly in the plan because…
options: the planner flattens simple views into the outer query
the view owns its own storage
MySQL forces inlining in every case
items.explain: Simple views are rewritten into the consuming query; only complex views (aggregates, DISTINCT, some joins) keep a Subquery Scan node.

blocks.md: The plan is where integrity meets the optimizer. A `CHECK` constraint can act as a guaranteed pre-condition during scans (and enables constraint exclusion on partitioned or inherited tables), and simple views vanish into the query that uses them.

blocks.title: CHECK constraint as a scan filter

blocks.md: **Constraints are pre-conditions the planner can exploit.** The `Filter: (price > 0)` reflects the guaranteed `CHECK`; on partitioned or inherited tables, constraint exclusion lets the planner skip entire children whose `CHECK` contradicts the query qualifier.

blocks.title: Aggregate over a view — the view is inlined

blocks.md: **Simple views flatten.** The plan references `subscriptions` directly, with the view's WHERE surfacing as a scan filter — no `Subquery Scan` node. Only complex views (aggregates, `DISTINCT`, some joins) can stay as `Subquery Scan`; an aggregate over a base view appears as `GroupAggregate` here because the view itself inlined.

items.q: The plan for SELECT status, count(*) FROM active_subscriptions GROUP BY status shows GroupAggregate over Seq Scan on subscriptions. Why is there no Subquery Scan node?
options: The view was flattened into the outer query
Views are always materialized as tables
GroupAggregate hides the view from the plan
MySQL never shows Subquery Scan nodes
items.explain: Simple views are inlined by the planner; only complex views keep a Subquery Scan node.

hints: Simple single-relation views flatten into the consuming query

items.title: Constraint-Conscious Planning
items.statement: products has CHECK (price > 0). Show via EXPLAIN where the Filter line appears for SELECT * FROM products WHERE price > 0, and explain how the planner exploits the constraint — including constraint exclusion on partitioned or inherited children whose CHECK contradicts a qualifier. State when no scan is needed at all.
hints: Expect Seq Scan ... Filter: (price > 0) — the constraint is a pre-condition
A qualifier that contradicts the CHECK (e.g., price < -1) can be answered without scanning
Constraint exclusion prunes partitioned/inherited children outright

revisionCard: EXCLUDE (GiST) bans cross-row patterns (range overlap); CHECK cannot see other rows
DEFERRABLE INITIALLY DEFERRED moves FK checks from statement end to COMMIT
1NF atomic + no repeating groups; 2NF no partial dependencies; 3NF no transitive dependencies; denormalize deliberately on read-hot facts
Simple views flatten into the outer query; security_invoker re-checks the caller; RLS filters rows and needs FORCE to cover the owner
ON DELETE CASCADE / SET NULL decide what happens to children when a parent disappears
Constraints are pre-conditions the planner exploits — filter lines, contradiction detection, constraint exclusion

glossary.def: A rule the database enforces (NOT NULL, UNIQUE, CHECK, FK, EXCLUDE) so that invalid rows cannot be written.
A GiST-based constraint that rejects a new row overlapping an existing row (e.g., range intersections).
A constraint whose check is postponed from statement end to transaction COMMIT.
Removing redundancy through 1NF/2NF/3NF decompositions so each fact lives in one place.
Deliberately re-joining tables (fact + dimension stars) to cut joins on read-heavy reporting paths.
Per-row filtering enforced by policies keyed to the current user or session context.
View option (PG 15+) that evaluates the calling user's privileges instead of the view owner's.
A column that depends on only part of a composite key — the 2NF violation.
